Nvidia in 2022 - PCIE power is obsolete, we are moving to a new power connector called 12VHPWR
Nvidia in 2025 - 12VHPWR isn't necessary for low end GPU's anymore, PCIE is fine shuv that back in to save costs.

aka - that 12VHPWR was such an absolute dumpster fire of a connector that Nvidia just gave up on it for GPU's that consume under 200W just to save their asses from more "GPU in flames" lawsuits...

tbh, i still don't quite understand what was the point of 12VHPWR to begin with?
the PCIE X8 power connector is capable of carrying up to 300W of power, and the motherboard PCIE connector is capable of carrying up to 75W of power (i believe modern motherboards and chipsets actually are now capable of carrying up to 150W on that PCIE Slot, and Asus's BTF motherboard can actually supply up to 650W from the PCIE slot + BTF connector)
so basically speaking, instead of introducing a new untested standard (that keeps frying GPU's for the past 3 years) Nvidia could've just specced their high power consumption cards with two 8 pin PCIE power connectors - and the PCIE Power standard should've just been updated to officially support up to 300W of power draw per 8 pin connector (the standard specs its a 250W connector but because it is such an overbuilt standard in reality it would actually support carrying 300W just fine)

i'd rather have had a RTX4090 or RTX5090 with two 8-Pin PCIE Power cables, heck even three 8-Pin PCIE power cables and have them not burst in flames, than have a single shitty small connector that has to be plugged in JUST RIGHT to not cause your power supply or 2000-4000$ GPU to burst into flames.

text: I know you guys are time constrained, but you missed something crucial. When you discussed memory bus bandwidth, you'll notice the 256 bit on the 3060ti is pcie 3.0. The 4060ti is 128 bit at pcie 4.0 (only 8 lanes used), and the 5060ti is 128 bit at pcie 5.0 (I'm assuming 8 lanes used again) with faster memory. Who buys this card? My guess is an AM4 user or older 9th to 11th gen intel user who may have had a prebuilt, or built a budget build back in the day. That being the case, checking performance relative to itself on pcie 4.0 and 3.0 would have been a great test. Even someone with an AMD 5600 may be on an older board limited to pcie 3.0 and will absolutely be throttled by bandwidth vs the test setup you guys have designed to take the cpu bottlenecks out of the equation. Re-running the test with forced lower pcie gen enabled in the bios would simulate it pretty well, but it would be 2 separate tests of tons of benchmarks just to compare this card against it's predecessors for older hardware users.

1: Never buy brand new.

2: Do you really need it?
Upgrade only if your current GPU can’t keep up.

3: Go back a gen, go high-end.
A strong last-gen GPU often beats a weak new-gen one at the same price.

4:Check real benchmarks, not hype.
Focus on actual performance in your games.

5:Make sure your system is balanced.
No point in a powerful GPU if your CPU bottlenecks.

6:Buy used with caution.
Check temps, performance, and history (mining?).

7:Wait for price drops after new releases.
Timing can save you serious cash.

8:Avoid small upgrades.
Skip a few generations – you’ll notice the difference more.

text: I will keep it simple, the problem is that you are restrained on the amount of Vram, becouse of the Memory Interface Width Nvidia chooses for its cards. ..to be fair Radeon cards of that time also had it for two generations (HyperMemory). Though they had more onboard VRAM (32-128MB)
